entities.summary:
Federico Savelli was a renowned Italian military commander who played a pivotal role in the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648), leading various armies for Catholic and Protestant forces.

Born in unknown circumstances, Savelli's early life remains shrouded in mystery. Despite this, his military prowess earned him recognition from European monarchs, including Emperor Ferdinand II of the Holy Roman Empire and Swedish King Gustav II Adolf.

Savelli's most notable achievement was his successful defense of the city of Mainz against a Protestant siege in 1631, which significantly contributed to the war's outcome. His leadership skills and tactical acumen made him a sought-after commander among European powers.

After the war, Savelli continued to serve as a military advisor to various rulers, influencing their strategies and shaping the course of European history. Despite his significant impact on the Thirty Years' War, Savelli's personal life remains largely unknown, adding to the enigma surrounding this important figure in early modern history.

The Savelli were one of Rome's most significant baronial families of the medieval and early modern periods, producing popes (Honorius III, Honorius IV), cardinals, and military commanders, and owning vast estates in the Castelli Romani (the hill towns southeast of Rome). Federico Savelli represents the family in its late phase — a member of the old Roman nobility navigating the political and military world of early modern Italy.

Federico Savelli served as a military commander in the service of various Italian powers and the Holy Roman Empire — the typical career path for members of the Roman baronial nobility in the early modern period, when the political fragmentation of Italy made military service to foreign powers the primary career option for Roman noble families outside the church.
